Skylab 3 took the endurance question and nearly doubled the answer. Where the first crew had stayed 28 days, Alan Bean's crew stayed 59 — pushing the human body further into long-duration weightlessness than anyone had gone, and returning healthier than the pessimists had feared. They logged a huge haul of solar observations from the Apollo Telescope Mount and rode out a scare when thruster leaks on their Apollo ferry briefly raised the prospect of a rescue flight. Skylab 3 is where long stays in space started to look not just survivable but routine — the quiet groundwork for every months-long station tour since.
Second Skylab crew — 59 days, deployed twin-pole solar shield to replace parasol

Bean, Garriott and Lousma — the second crew to live aboard Skylab, for 59 days 11 hours. Launched 1973-07-28 11:11 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-207). On approach to the station, an attitude-control thruster quad on the CSM service module leaked; after a second quad leaked about six days later, back-up CSM-119 was prepped at Cape Canaveral for a possible rescue mission, but the crew completed nominally. Garriott led about 305 crew-hours of solar observations using the Apollo Telescope Mount instruments. Three EVAs deployed a twin-pole sun shield over the original parasol, repaired the rate gyro package, and recovered film canisters from the ATM. Splashed down 1973-09-25 22:19 UTC; CSM-117 displayed at the Glenn Visitor Center, Cleveland.
Saturn IB SA-207 from LC-39B 1973-07-28 11:11 UTC.
Second service-module RCS quad leak (the first was on approach); rescue CSM-119 prepared at Cape but not flown.
Crew deployed twin-pole shield over original parasol.
CSM-117 splashed down in Pacific 1973-09-25 22:19 UTC.
